slides.title: Hazards Assessment Report
slides.subtitle: Naples, Italy
textBlocks: Group Presentation | Hazards, Risk & Mitigation

Big Question
How do Earth systems influence the hazards present to people living in different locations?
Mount Vesuvius and Naples waterfront

Team members and focus areas
Mariet Young - Priorities, mitigation & integration; Volcanoes
Saniah Mcwilliams - Tectonics & geography
Stephanie Xiong-Cha - Earthquakes & ground response
Stacey Konde - Climate change

slides.title: Part I: Tectonics & geography
slides.subtitle: Saniah McWilliams
textBlocks: Naples’ hazards begin with a complex central Mediterranean plate setting.
Central Mediterranean plate interaction

Key interpretation:
Africa/Nubia slowly moves toward Eurasia across the Mediterranean.
The Adriatic/Apulian microplate makes southern Italy a complex deformation zone.
Compression + extension help produce both earthquakes and volcanism near Naples.
Africa/Nubia → Eurasia + Apulian microplate = earthquakes + volcanoes
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: Saniah McWilliams presentation; Herman et al. (2015); Di Bucci et al. (2010); Serpelloni et al. (2007).

slides.title: Tectonic plates shaping Naples
slides.subtitle: Saniah McWilliams
textBlocks: Which plates, motion, and boundary style influence the region?
Africa / Nubia
Eurasia
Apulian microplate

Complex deformation zone
compression + extension + faulting

Result for Naples
Plate motion creates crustal stress and fractures; extension helps open pathways for magma and hydrothermal fluids.
This is why Naples has overlapping hazards: regional earthquakes, volcanic unrest, ground deformation, and coastal exposure.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: Saniah McWilliams presentation; Herman et al. (2015); USGS/YVO (2023).

slides.title: Topography & geography concentrate risk
slides.subtitle: Saniah McWilliams
textBlocks: Naples is built between active volcanic systems, dense coastal development, and the Gulf of Naples.
Map area: Naples, Gulf of Naples, Vesuvius, Campi Flegrei, and Ischia

Why this matters
Campi Flegrei lies west of Naples; Mount Vesuvius is east/southeast of the city.
The Gulf of Naples and dense coastal development can make evacuation difficult.
Risk is high because millions of people live close to active volcanic systems.
Hazards are not isolated; they overlap with a crowded urban area.
Council message: geography turns Earth processes into urban risk.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: Saniah McWilliams presentation; USGS/YVO (2023); Carlino (2021).

slides.title: How tectonics create Naples hazards
slides.subtitle: Saniah McWilliams
textBlocks: Plate motion connects directly to earthquakes, volcanism, and hydrothermal unrest.

Plate motion
Africa/Nubia → Eurasia

Crustal stress
faulting + stretching

Magma & heat
volcanic systems

Hydrothermal pressure
groundwater + gas

Hazards
earthquakes + unrest

Science connection
Tectonic stress creates faults that can slip and produce earthquakes.
Extension and heat help feed Campi Flegrei and Vesuvius volcanic systems.
Hot fluids and gas contribute to bradyseism, shallow quakes, and hydrothermal hazards.
Regional earthquake-depth pattern: Italy and surrounding plate systems
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: Saniah McWilliams presentation; Herman et al. (2015); Smithsonian Global Volcanism Program; USGS/YVO (2023).

slides.title: Part I takeaway: Earth systems create place-specific hazards
slides.subtitle: Saniah McWilliams
textBlocks: Answering the Big Question for Naples starts with plate tectonics.
Africa–Eurasia convergence creates a broad, complex boundary.
The Apulian microplate and Apennines focus deformation near southern Italy.
Extension + subduction-related processes help produce magma and heat.
People live on a coast between active volcanoes and earthquake sources.
Hazards are not random in Naples—they reflect how tectonics, volcanism, geography, and population overlap.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Synthesis based on Part I sources and Saniah McWilliams presentation.

slides.title: Part II: Earthquakes and ground response
slides.subtitle: Stephanie Xiong-Cha
textBlocks: Earthquake history, faults, ground conditions, secondary hazards, and exposure
Campi Flegrei / Naples ground-shaking and seismicity context

Focus questions
What earthquake sources are most likely to affect Naples?
Which ground conditions can make shaking worse?
Where are people, buildings, and infrastructure most exposed?

Part II approach
Use INGV and IRIS/EarthScope earthquake mapping for seismicity.
Connect shaking risk to bradyseism, faults, and volcanic unrest.
Evaluate ground response, secondary hazards, population, and infrastructure exposure.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: Stephanie Xiong-Cha presentation; Herman et al. (2015); IRIS/EarthScope; INGV/Osservatorio Vesuviano; Dipartimento della Protezione Civile.

slides.title: Earthquake type, location, magnitude, and frequency
slides.subtitle: Stephanie Xiong-Cha
textBlocks: Naples is affected by regional tectonic earthquakes and shallow volcano-tectonic earthquakes.
Regional seismicity map for southern Italy; use IRIS/EarthScope to re-export if needed

Stephanie’s key points
Type: volcano-tectonic activity linked to Campi Flegrei bradyseism, plus regional tectonic sources.
Location: Astroni, Solfatara–Pisciarelli–Agnano, Pozzuoli, and the Gulf of Pozzuoli are active local areas.
Magnitude: recent local events have reached about M4.6, but regional Apennine earthquakes can be larger.
Frequency: small local quakes are recurring during unrest; larger M6–7 regional earthquakes are rarer but high consequence.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: Stephanie Xiong-Cha presentation; INGV; Herman et al. (2015); IRIS/EarthScope Interactive Earthquake Browser; INGV CPTI15–DBMI15 catalogue.

slides.title: Magnitude pattern: most events are moderate, but shallow
slides.subtitle: Stephanie Xiong-Cha
textBlocks: Recent earthquake records show many smaller events and fewer larger events near Naples / Campi Flegrei.

Interpretation
Most recorded events fall in the lower-magnitude classes, which fits a volcano-unrest setting with many small shocks.
Even lower-magnitude earthquakes can be disruptive when they are very shallow and directly beneath populated areas.
Risk ranking should consider exposure and ground response, not magnitude alone.
Presentation point: a smaller shallow earthquake near Pozzuoli or western Naples can cause more local concern than a larger event farther away.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Source: Stephanie Xiong-Cha presentation earthquake-count table; INGV/CPTI15–DBMI15 for earthquake-catalogue context.

slides.title: Surface materials and shake response
slides.subtitle: Stephanie Xiong-Cha
textBlocks: Local geology explains why shaking damage varies by neighborhood.
Real INGV/PGA ground-shaking map for Campi Flegrei area

Ground-response findings
Neapolitan Yellow Tuff has been used as “building stone” since ancient times and is common in the urban fabric.
Volcanic tuff, ash, pumice, and pyroclastic deposits can respond differently from stronger bedrock during shaking.
Coastal lowlands and artificial fill can amplify shaking and may increase liquefaction concern.
Older or fragile buildings, infrastructure, and cultural heritage increase vulnerability.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: Stephanie Xiong-Cha presentation; Morra et al. (2010); ISPRA / Servizio Geologico d’Italia geological mapping; Herman et al. (2015).

slides.title: Faults and seismic sources affecting Naples
slides.subtitle: Stephanie Xiong-Cha
textBlocks: Regional faults and local caldera structures both affect Naples.
Real INGV Campi Flegrei seismic monitoring / source-area map

Key fault/source areas
Southern Apennine normal faults: regional source of larger tectonic earthquakes affecting Campania.
Campi Flegrei caldera faults: shallow local source tied to bradyseism and volcanic unrest.
Irpinia fault system: example of a damaging regional earthquake source east of Naples.
Vesuvius and Ischia add local volcano-seismic source areas.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: Stephanie Xiong-Cha presentation; DISS Working Group / INGV Database of Individual Seismogenic Sources; Herman et al. (2015).

slides.title: Earthquake-related hazards beyond shaking
slides.subtitle: Stephanie Xiong-Cha
textBlocks: Secondary hazards can disrupt transportation, utilities, and emergency response.
Real satellite map of Bay of Naples earthquake-related hazard context

Hazard summary
Ground shaking is metro-wide, especially where soft sediments or volcanic deposits amplify motion.
Liquefaction is most likely in low-lying coastal, alluvial, and reclaimed harbor/waterfront areas.
Landslides and rockfall are concerns on steep crater margins, Vesuvius slopes, and the Sorrento Peninsula.
Tsunami or harbor seiche hazards are lower probability but possible from offshore earthquakes or submarine landslides.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: Stephanie Xiong-Cha presentation; INGV Osservatorio Vesuviano ShakeMap; Dipartimento della Protezione Civile vulnerability and microzonation plan; USGS hazard context.

slides.title: Observed ground shaking: Campi Flegrei event
slides.subtitle: Stephanie Xiong-Cha
textBlocks: Recent INGV data show why shallow local earthquakes matter for Naples-area planning.
INGV station map / PGA values for Campi Flegrei ground-shaking context

Why this map matters
The strongest shaking is localized near the Campi Flegrei source area, west of central Naples.
Urban districts around Pozzuoli, Bagnoli, Agnano, and western Naples need priority inspection and communication planning.
Peak ground acceleration maps help identify where structures and lifelines may need rapid post-event checks.
This supports mitigation focused on vulnerable buildings, schools, hospitals, utilities, and evacuation routes.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: Stephanie Xiong-Cha presentation; INGV Osservatorio Vesuviano ShakeMap / PGA context; Martino et al. (2025).

slides.title: Population exposure and likely loss concentration
slides.subtitle: Stephanie Xiong-Cha
textBlocks: Risk is highest where shaking, older buildings, and infrastructure overlap.
Real Naples–Campi Flegrei–Vesuvius location map with population-density inset

Exposure takeaways
Naples, Pozzuoli, Bacoli, Portici, Ercolano, Torre del Greco, and Torre Annunziata are priority planning communities.
USGS notes that more than 3.5 million people live within about 30 km of the Naples volcanic-seismic system.
Critical exposure includes ports, roads, rail, hospitals, schools, utilities, and the historic center.
A severe regional earthquake could plausibly cause multi-billion-euro losses and long disruption to housing and lifelines.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: Stephanie Xiong-Cha presentation; USGS/YVO (2023) population context; Dipartimento della Protezione Civile vulnerability plan. Cost is a classroom planning estimate, not an official loss model.

slides.title: Part III-A: Volcanoes
slides.subtitle: Mariet Young
textBlocks: Volcanoes: eruption history, exposure, and risk
Volcanoes section

• Locate and classify the major volcanic features: Campi Flegrei caldera, Mount Vesuvius stratovolcano, and Ischia volcanic island.
• Use photos/maps to show how volcanic landforms overlap with dense population and evacuation routes.
• Summarize eruption history and the 100-year planning outlook without claiming exact prediction.
• Identify vulnerable locations, likely hazards, population exposure, and estimated disaster cost.

slides.title: Volcanoes around Naples: location and volcanic features
slides.subtitle: Naples sits between three active volcanic systems: Campi Flegrei, Vesuvius, and Ischia.
textBlocks: Campi Flegrei: caldera
Vesuvius: stratovolcano
Ischia: volcanic island

Why this matters
• Campi Flegrei is a broad caldera partly beneath western Naples and Pozzuoli Bay; it is not a single cone.
• Vesuvius is a steep stratovolcano southeast of Naples with a history of explosive eruptions.
• Ischia is an offshore volcanic island with both eruption and earthquake history.
• Different volcanic forms create different hazards: pyroclastic flows, ash fall, lava, gas, hydrothermal explosions, ground deformation, and volcano-tectonic earthquakes.
Mariet Young
slides.section: Part III — Volcanoes and Climate Change

slides.title: Pictures of volcanic features in the region
slides.subtitle: The most visible volcanic hazard is Vesuvius, but Campi Flegrei affects the western urban area more directly.
textBlocks: Mount Vesuvius crater
ESA ISS image of Mount Vesuvius: crater and dense settlement around the slopes.
Campi Flegrei caldera
Campi Flegrei is not a single cone; it is a caldera with vents, craters, and hydrothermal areas embedded in the city.

Presentation point
• City officials should not think only about Vesuvius. The highest planning concern is the overlap of several volcanic systems with dense urban neighborhoods, hospitals, ports, roads, and evacuation routes.
Mariet Young

100-year eruption outlook
• Campi Flegrei: eruption probability is not zero; ongoing unrest means close monitoring and evacuation planning are essential.
• Vesuvius: currently quiet but active; future eruption is expected eventually, but timing is uncertain.
• Ischia: lower eruption probability than Campi Flegrei or Vesuvius, but local volcanic earthquakes remain important.
• Planning should use monitoring alert levels, hazard zones, and evacuation triggers rather than exact eruption prediction.

Planning interpretation
• Rank volcanic hazards by consequence × exposure × warning time.
• Even a moderate explosive eruption could force mass evacuation and regional disruption.
• The practical decision tools are alert levels, evacuation zones, drills, and public communication.
Mariet Young

slides.title: Most vulnerable volcanic locations and likely hazards
slides.subtitle: Greatest volcanic risk follows the red/yellow emergency zones and the dense coastal corridor around Naples.
textBlocks: CF red-zone communities
Vesuvius zone

Most likely volcanic hazards
• Pyroclastic density currents: fastest and deadliest eruption hazard; evacuation before eruption is the main life-safety measure.
• Ash/lapilli fall: roof collapse, air-quality problems, transport shutdowns, water contamination, and power disruption.
• Volcano-tectonic earthquakes and bradyseism: cracking, structural damage, repeated disruption, and public anxiety.
• Hydrothermal explosions and gas: localized but dangerous near Solfatara/Pisciarelli and other vent areas.
• Lahars/debris flows: most concerning on Vesuvius slopes and drainage channels after heavy rainfall.
Mariet Young

slides.title: Volcanic disaster exposure: population affected and cost
slides.subtitle: The population at risk is unusually high because volcanic zones overlap with the Naples metropolitan area.
textBlocks:
Campi Flegrei red-zone residents
require precautionary evacuation

Vesuvius red-zone residents
face evacuation in eruption crisis
>3 million

People within 20 km of possible vents
in the Naples volcanic area

Likely disaster costs
• Direct costs: evacuation logistics, sheltering, ash cleanup, building damage, utility repairs, and road/rail closure.
• Indirect costs: lost tourism, port disruption, business interruption, school/hospital displacement, and long-term relocation.
• Planning estimate: a major volcanic crisis could plausibly create multi-billion-euro losses even if evacuation prevents mass fatalities.

Most affected places
• Campi Flegrei: Pozzuoli, Bacoli, Quarto, Monte di Procida, and western Naples neighborhoods.
• Vesuvius: towns on the volcano flanks plus ash-fall communities downwind.
• Critical systems: port, rail/road corridors, hospitals, schools, water/power systems, and tourism routes.
Mariet Young

slides.title: Part III-B: Climate Change
slides.subtitle: Stacey Konde
textBlocks: Climate change: heat, flooding, drought, and sea-level exposure
What Stacey’s slides add

Climate risk is already visible through dangerous heat events in Italy.
By 2100, port and waterfront flooding become a larger planning concern.
These climate hazards affect public health, tourism, transportation, utilities, and emergency response.
slides.section: Part III — Volcanoes and Climate Change
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Source base: https://www.noaa.gov/education/resource-collections/climate/climate-change-impacts

slides.title: Climate Change: heat risk in Naples
slides.subtitle: Stacey Konde
textBlocks: Naples can get hot — heat risk is a public-health hazard
Key message

Hotter summers increase heat illness, cooling demand, power stress, and risk to elderly and low-income residents.
Urban areas like Naples can experience stronger heat stress because pavement and dense buildings store heat.
Mitigation connection: heat warnings, cooling centers, shade, trees, water access, and checks on vulnerable residents.
slides.section: Part III — Volcanoes and Climate Change

slides.title: Climate Change: heat is already happening
slides.subtitle: Stacey Konde
textBlocks: Summer 2022 showed why heat planning matters
Summer 2022 a record-Breaking Heat Across Italy happened:

Causing Approximately 18,010 heat-related deaths during the summer of 2022.
Italy recorded one of the highest heat-related mortality rates in Europe (about 295 deaths per million people).
These findings highlight the need for heat action plans, cooling centers, and improved emergency preparedness in cities like Naples.
Planning implication for Naples

Heat action plans, cooling centers, and public alerts should be treated as hazard mitigation, not just weather advice.
Heat preparedness supports the final mitigation plan because it saves lives during events that are becoming more frequent.
slides.section: Part III — Volcanoes and Climate Change
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Stacey Presentation.pdf heat mortality slide; Ballester et al. (2023), Nature Medicine, heat-related mortality in Europe during summer 2022.

slides.title: Climate Change: sea-level rise and flooding
slides.subtitle: Stacey Konde
textBlocks: Port and waterfront flooding are key climate-change exposure points
Stacey planning value
Most exposed
Port / waterfront
Why it matters

Higher sea level can make storm surge, coastal flooding, and drainage backups more damaging.
The port, waterfront roads, tourism areas, utilities, and emergency routes are vulnerable because they sit near the Bay of Naples.
This connects climate change to economic disruption, not only environmental change.
Stacey Presentation.pdf flooding slide; NASA/IPCC sea-level projection resources and Climate Central listed in Stacey references.

slides.title: Climate change projections: temperature and precipitation
slides.subtitle: By 2050 and 2100, Campania is projected to get warmer, drier overall, and more prone to intense rainfall events.
textBlocks: Interpretation for Naples: heat stress, cooling demand, drought risk, and short-duration heavy rain all increase. Stacey's climate draft adds a real-world example: the 2022 heat wave across Italy shows why Naples needs heat alerts, cooling centers, and emergency preparedness.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: Giugliano et al. (2022); IPCC AR6 Mediterranean Region (2022); Stacey draft citing Ballester et al. (2023).

slides.title: Climate change: sea level rise, flooding, and drought
slides.subtitle: Naples is coastal, so climate risk includes compound flooding: sea level rise + storm surge + intense rainfall + drainage limits.
textBlocks: Riverine flood risk + population
Campania coastal inundation

2100 planning range for city officials: about 1-3.6 ft (0.3-1.1 m) of sea-level rise under low-to-high emissions, plus local vertical ground motion from tectonic/volcanic processes. Main impacts: port flooding, drainage backflow, storm surge, and road/utility disruption.
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: NASA Sea Level Projection Tool / IPCC AR6; Di Paola et al. (2021); PERI-CENE Naples flood-risk map using GHSL and WRI Aqueduct data; Stacey climate draft.

slides.title: Mariet Young
slides.subtitle: Part IV: Priorities, Mitigation & Integration
textBlocks: Turn the science into a city-council decision.
This section integrates tectonics, earthquake history, volcano risk, climate projections, exposure, and economics into one prioritized mitigation plan.
Prioritize
Rank the hazards using a transparent scoring method.
Mitigate
Recommend one integrated 10-year readiness and retrofit program.
Act
Ask the council to approve funding, inspections, and public drills.
Workflow source: Naples Hazards final briefing plan, slides 14–18; scenario values are classroom planning estimates.

slides.title: Integration: why one plan must address several hazards
slides.subtitle: Naples’ top hazards are connected through Earth systems, urban exposure, and shared evacuation/lifeline needs.
textBlocks: Plate tectonics → earthquakes
Regional faults + shallow volcanic quakes create shaking, liquefaction, landslide risk.
Magma + hydrothermal systems
Campi Flegrei and Vesuvius create pyroclastic flow, ash, gas, and unrest hazards.
Topography + surface materials
Coastal fill, tuff, slopes, and dense basins amplify impacts and complicate evacuation.
Climate change + coast
Sea-level rise, heat, drought, and intense rainfall stress the same lifelines.
Integrated risk management
Same people, roads, hospitals, utilities, and warning systems are exposed to multiple hazards.

Takeaway for the council
Do not fund separate one-hazard plans; fund a single program that upgrades buildings, routes, alerts, shelters, drills, and critical lifelines together.
Mariet Young
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: Herman et al. (2015); Civil Protection Department emergency planning maps; Iervolino et al. (2024); IPCC/NASA sea-level sources used in Part III.

slides.title: 10-year Multi-Hazard Readiness and Retrofit Program
slides.subtitle: One mitigation strategy that reduces losses across the top four hazards.
textBlocks:
Plan description
Focus first on Campi Flegrei/western Naples, schools, hospitals, evacuation routes, port access, and older buildings.
Combine seismic retrofit, ash-load roof checks, flood/drainage upgrades, alerts, shelters, route signs, and annual drills.

Implementation needs
Municipal engineering teams
INGV/Civil Protection coordination
Building inventory database
Public outreach in multiple languages

Expected effectiveness
Reduces collapse risk and displacement
Shortens evacuation time
Keeps hospitals, port access, and emergency routes functioning
Protects residents before the alarm phase

slides.title: Cost-benefit and call to action
slides.subtitle: The highest-value decision is to invest before warning time is short.
textBlocks: Planning estimate: what the investment buys
10-year readiness + retrofit program
Lives saved
Early warning + drills + retrofit
Displacement reduced
Safer buildings + shelters + routes
Economic losses avoided
Port, roads, hospitals, utilities protected

Expected risk reduction
Preventive evacuation can keep volcanic-death totals low if residents know routes and warnings are trusted.
Retrofitting the most critical buildings first can reduce collapse-related injuries and shelter demand.
Flood/drainage and backup-power work protects day-to-day services and post-disaster recovery.
Decision request to city council
Approve
Start Phase 1 hazard mapping, building inventory, and priority inspections.
Fund
Create a 10-year capital program with annual progress reporting.
Practice
Require annual evacuation/shelter drills for schools, hospitals, port, and neighborhoods.
Call for action: approve Phase 1 within the next budget cycle, before the next volcanic unrest or earthquake crisis limits choices.
Mariet Young
slides.sourceOrCitationText: Sources: Civil Protection emergency planning; Iervolino et al. (2024); National Institute of Building Sciences (2019). Budget is a classroom planning range, not an official municipal estimate.
